## Simple explanation

Binary classification predicts which of two categories applies to an
example, such as whether an email is spam or not spam.

## Technical explanation

A binary classifier produces a score or probability for one class, then
uses a decision threshold to assign a label. Models may be trained with
losses such as binary cross-entropy. The threshold and class definitions
should reflect the costs of false positives and false negatives.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Binary classification appears in fraud detection, moderation, medical
screening, and quality checks. Accuracy alone can be misleading when class
frequencies or error costs are unequal, so evaluation should also consider
precision, recall, calibration, and the operating threshold.

## How it works

The model maps input features to a score, often transformed into a
probability $p$. A threshold $\tau$ determines the predicted class:
predict the positive class when $p \geq \tau$. During training, the model's
parameters are adjusted to reduce a classification loss.

## Practical example

A simple image classifier can predict whether a photo shows a penguin or an
ostrich. The accompanying [fast.ai notebook](../../notebooks/B/binary-classification.ipynb)
is a beginner-friendly scaffold for building and evaluating this model.
It contains Markdown instructions only; fill in the code as you work
through the exercise.

## Common misconceptions

- A score is not necessarily a calibrated probability.
- A threshold of 0.5 is not always appropriate.
- High accuracy can hide poor performance on a rare class.
